title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.1 Harm Is Contested, Not Measured
Which is more dangerous: alcohol or cannabis? Most people answer on the basis of what is legal, and the law does not match the evidence. Alcohol kills hundreds of thousands of people a year and sits in supermarkets; cannabis, with a lower measured harm profile, was a criminal offense for most of a century, and its enforcement fell almost entirely on Black and Latino communities. The point is not which substance is worse; it is that the law does not first measure harm and then regulate it. We first decide who and what matters, then find or manufacture the harm that justifies the decision.
Four cases show how harm is contested rather than measured. Consider sex. What was “private” versus what was “criminal” has been redrawn case by case, in someone’s interests, with no consistent underlying principle. Sexual behavior between consenting adults was criminally regulated well into the twentieth century, and the expansion of privacy was won, not discovered. Sodomy laws are a Victorian legal export, written in 1861 and 1885, and used to convict Oscar Wilde before spreading through colonial law; they are not an ancient universal. Marital rape was legal in most US states until the 1970s and 1980s, because the private sphere was the household, not the person.
Consider drugs. Portugal decriminalized personal possession of all drugs in 2001, pairing the change with treatment and harm reduction; HIV transmission and overdose deaths fell, and use did not rise. Consider guns. After the Columbine shootings, legislators went after violent video games, but the evidence never supported that hypothesis, and cross-national comparisons point to gun availability, inequality, and the history of racially organized violence as the real drivers. Consider privacy. Its historical unit was the household, not the person, and what counts as a protected sphere is won and redrawn, not discovered.
The common thread is that harm is a claim made by the powerful, the panicked, and the organized, not a fact that precedes regulation.

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.2 Two Models of Harm
Engineers are trained on a particular model of failure: the faulty valve that causes a boiler explosion. Harm in this model is rare, dramatic, and attributable. But the worst damage caused by industry has not worked this way. When leaded gasoline lowered the IQs of an entire generation of children, no single tank of fuel caused a measurable injury. No particular cigarette caused any particular cancer death. The harm is real and massive, but it is distributed across millions of small exposures, so that no single decision can be shown to have caused a single injury.
Social media’s harms are this second kind. The term cognitive pollution captures the pattern: radicalization, depression, and polarization are byproducts of engagement maximization, produced at scale and priced at zero. The causal chain is long, probabilistic, and hard to attribute, which is exactly what makes it hard to regulate. The philosopher Derek Parfit identified the philosophical twin of this problem: the non-identity problem. If our choices change who is born, then no particular future person can say we made them worse off, yet the choice still has victims in the aggregate. Harms to “future people” cannot name an individual victim, which is why they are so easy to postpone.
Once a society accepts that harm can be diffuse and cumulative, responsibility shifts from proving individual causation to holding the emitter accountable for the aggregate. Engineers now study pollution not out of conscience but because liability eventually forced them to.
The shift has a legal consequence. If harm is rare, dramatic, and attributable, responsible engineering means avoiding the specific decision that produces the failure. Under the pollution model, responsible engineers are accountable for long-term cumulative effects. A few recent court judgments in the United States suggest this shift is finally happening, but they will be contested, and as the overturn of Roe v. Wade shows, precedent is not a guarantee. Legislation that holds tech companies responsible for the damage their products do to users’ mental health can come sooner, will be more robust, and will have more impact than gestures like banning young people from social media.
The law has mostly not solved the problem of future harm either, which explains why our legal obligations to future people are so weak. Courts require an identifiable party who has suffered a concrete injury. Future generations fail this test on both counts. The workarounds are real but imperfect. Environmental impact assessments require governments to consider long-term consequences. Some constitutions are designed to be difficult to amend. In 1993, the Philippine Supreme Court allowed a group of children to sue the government on behalf of future generations in Oposa v. Factoran. Wales and Hungary have created parliamentary commissioners tasked with representing future interests. These are genuine innovations, but today’s legislators still have no electoral incentive to sacrifice for people who cannot vote.

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.3 The Uncertainty Playbook
When a harm is alleged, the standard industry playbook runs in five steps: fund scientists to generate alternative hypotheses, insist that correlation is not causation, describe any call for regulation as an attack on freedom, create front organizations with neutral-sounding names, and delay—because delay is profit. The response then moves through four phases: denial, uncertainty, the market argument, and finally acceptance, at which point compliance reliably turns out to be cheaper than predicted.
The tobacco industry wrote the script. In 1950, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill published a landmark study linking smoking to lung cancer. The industry’s response was a masterclass in making clear things seem murky: it formed a research committee, funded scientists, and insisted for decades that the evidence was inconclusive. Internal documents later proved the executives knew the risks long before the public did. Within four years, American cigarette manufacturers had formed the Tobacco Industry Research Committee, later renamed the Council for Tobacco Research. They hired scientists, funded studies, placed ads in newspapers, and issued press releases arguing that the evidence was inconclusive. Their goal was not to disprove the science: it was to create enough uncertainty that politicians felt they could not act and smokers felt they could not be sure. The same script ran for leaded gasoline, asbestos, and oxycontin, and it is running now for social media and AI (Oreskes and Conway 2010).
The argument from the market deserves special attention, because it fails in every case where it has been tested. Consumers cannot evaluate a placental crossing rate for a sedative, or the probability that a suspension design will cause a rollover, or the structural integrity of a crumple zone. Markets aggregate preferences for things people can evaluate; they do not reliably handle latent hazards that require technical expertise and longitudinal data to detect.

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.4 When Regulation Works
The history of pollution shows what regulation looks like when it succeeds. In December 1952, a coal-smog blanketed London so thick that people could not see their own feet, killing at least 4,000 people in four days— a figure researchers later revised to closer to 12,000. The government’s first response was to blame influenza, but the Clean Air Act of 1956 followed, and the great smogs did not return. On June 22, 1969, the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland caught fire— the thirteenth time it had done so since 1868— and the resulting photograph helped produce the Clean Water Act of 1972. The Thames had been an open sewer since the Great Stink of 1858, but enforceable sewage-treatment requirements turned it around, and in 1983 a salmon was caught in the river for the first time since the 1820s. In every case, what changed was not public disgust, which had existed for a century, but the legal and economic cost of pollution.
The same lesson can be read backwards. At Minamata Bay in Japan, the Chisso chemical company discharged mercury for decades; cats, which ate fish scraps, sickened first and were ignored as an early warning, and official recognition of the disease came only in 1968, more than a decade after the symptoms appeared. A cross-border disaster can sometimes be converted into enforceable rules: after a 1986 fire at a Sandoz warehouse sent thirty tonnes of pesticides into the Rhine, the Rhine Action Programme set binding pollution targets, and salmon returned to the river within a decade.
The pharmaceutical parallel is the precautionary principle. Thalidomide was approved in West Germany in 1957 and sold in forty-six countries, but Frances Kelsey, a pharmacologist at the US Food and Drug Administration, refused to approve it because the safety evidence was insufficient. The birth defects that followed where it was approved vindicated her, and the Kefauver-Harris Amendment of 1962 followed. Before it, you could sell a drug in the United States without proving it did anything; after it, you had to show that it worked. Where harm is plausible and irreversible, the burden of proof may rest on those introducing the risk.
Product safety tells the same story. Ralph Nader’s 1965 book accused General Motors of selling cars it knew to be dangerous; GM’s response was to hire private detectives to dig up dirt on him, and when the surveillance was exposed, GM’s president had to apologize on national television, and Congress passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act that same year (Nader 1965). Sweden mandated front seatbelts in new cars in 1959. The evidence for their effectiveness was already solid: Nils Bohlin, an engineer at Volvo, had developed the three-point belt the year before, and Volvo had made the patent freely available to every manufacturer. This was not altruism—Volvo wanted to market its cars as safe—but the effect was the same. The United States did not require seatbelts in new cars until 1968, and individual states did not begin requiring drivers to wear them until the 1980s. Australia’s Victoria became the first jurisdiction anywhere in the world to require seatbelt use in 1970—a decade before most American states. Airbags, first demonstrated as viable technology in the 1950s, were not required in all new American passenger cars until 1998. At every step, car makers argued that the requirement was premature, that consumers would choose safety features if they really wanted them, and that regulation would raise costs and kill innovation. At every step, the data showed substantial reductions in deaths after regulations changed. When buyers compare cars, they mostly look at price, fuel economy, and styling. They do not systematically seek out crash-test ratings. This is not a character flaw; it is a predictable feature of how people make decisions under uncertainty about low-probability events.
The hardest lesson is that a disaster alone does not produce regulation. The Triangle Shirtwaist fire of 1911 killed 146 workers behind locked stairwell doors, and the owners were acquitted and collected the insurance; what turned the fire into fifty-six pieces of legislation— recounted in full in the next chapter—was the fire plus the unions and reform organizations that could turn grief into legislative pressure (Orleck 1995).

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.5 The Ozone Hole That Closed
In 1974, two chemists at the University of California published a paper predicting that chlorofluorocarbons would destroy the ozone layer that shields Earth from ultraviolet radiation. CFCs were used as propellants in aerosol cans and refrigerants in air conditioners, and while the paper’s authors did not yet have a hole to point to, they had atmospheric chemistry on their side.
The chemical industry’s response was to fund counter-research, hire lobbyists, and describe the scientists as alarmists whose work was too speculative to justify regulatory action. This was the same playbook the tobacco industry had been running for two decades, and for a while it worked. The Alliance for Responsible CFC Policy argued that the science was uncertain. Industry representatives testified before Congress that banning CFCs would cost hundreds of thousands of jobs. Du Pont, which held a large share of the CFC market, said in 1975 that it would stop making CFCs only if a worldwide scientific consensus emerged and the appropriate regulatory bodies took action. This was not a promise to act; it was a description of conditions the company presumably believed would never be met.
Eleven years later, in 1985, a team from the British Antarctic Survey reported a massive thinning of the ozone layer over Antarctica every southern spring. Their data was so far outside expected ranges that they initially assumed their instruments were broken. NASA confirmed the finding using satellite data that had been sitting in archived files for years, after automated quality-control software had flagged the anomalous readings as errors.
Industry resistance collapsed in just two years, and the Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987. Its design explains why it worked when so many other environmental agreements have not. It set binding phase-out schedules for ozone-depleting substances, with different timelines for developed and developing countries. It established trade sanctions against non-signatories, which meant that countries outside the agreement faced economic costs for staying out. And it created the Multilateral Fund, which transferred technology and money from wealthy countries to developing ones. This last element gets the least attention and does the most work.
When the protocol was negotiated, China and India were skeptical. Both were industrializing rapidly, both had growing demand for refrigeration and air conditioning, and both pointed out that the damage to the ozone layer had been caused almost entirely by wealthy countries. The demand that they now forgo the same technologies their competitors had used looked like a way of keeping them poor. The Multilateral Fund changed the calculation. By 2023 it had disbursed over $4 billion to help developing countries transition away from CFCs. China became one of the largest recipients of technology transfer funding and one of the most consistent compliers with phase-out schedules. Neither country did this because its leaders suddenly became environmentalists: compliance became economically rational once the fund made alternatives affordable.
Du Pont, which had spent years arguing that alternatives were technically impossible, announced shortly after the protocol was signed that it had developed workable substitutes and would accelerate their commercialization. What had been technically impossible became technically straightforward once the regulatory framework made the old product unmarketable.
The substitutes were hydrofluorocarbons. They did not destroy the ozone layer, but they turned out to be extremely potent greenhouse gases, some thousands of times more warming per molecule than carbon dioxide. The Kigali Amendment, adopted in 2016, added HFCs to the list of controlled substances and set phase-down schedules for them. Climate scientists estimated that full implementation would avoid up to 0.4°C of warming by 2100.
This is not a story about individual consumers making better choices. Millions of people did not read scientific papers and switch to pump-action hairspray. The mechanism was a binding international agreement with differentiated obligations, a technology transfer fund, and trade sanctions against non-participants.

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.6 Settlement Versus Solution
The 1998 Master Settlement Agreement is the cautionary tale. Forty-six states sued the tobacco companies to recover $206 billion in Medicaid costs, and won. But it was a settlement, not a solution: it monetized the harm rather than removing it, and the industry survived and moved into new markets.
The road to that settlement ran through the Surgeon General’s report of 1964, fourteen years after Doll and Hill’s paper, which stated clearly that smoking caused lung cancer and recommended action. The industry spent the next thirty-four years fighting a rear-guard action. What eventually forced a reckoning was a combination of litigation, public health advocacy, investigative journalism, congressional hearings, and the slow accumulation of economic costs borne by state Medicaid programs. The key legal move was a shift in how states argued their cases. Rather than proving that smoking had harmed specific individuals, which the industry could defeat by arguing about individual risk tolerance, states sued to recover the cost of treating sick smokers. Mississippi was first in 1994, and by 1998 forty-six states had reached the Master Settlement Agreement.
It was a victory, but it took forty years to go from a clear scientific finding to a partial legal resolution, and even then the industry survived and moved into new markets. Other countries responded slowly, but they did respond. Australia required plain packaging for all tobacco products in 2012: no logos, no distinctive colors, just the brand name in a standardized font on a drab olive-brown background, surrounded by graphic health warnings. The industry challenged the law in the High Court and lost unanimously. Philip Morris then filed a challenge under an investor protection treaty between Hong Kong and Australia, arguing that plain packaging violated the treaty’s provisions on foreign investors. The tribunal dismissed it in 2015 on the grounds that Philip Morris had restructured its Australian operations specifically to gain access to the treaty—a move so transparently opportunistic that even the arbitrators were not impressed. What eventually made the difference was not better science but organized pressure operating through multiple channels simultaneously: litigation, public health campaigns, investigative journalism, and international organizations like the World Health Organization, whose Framework Convention on Tobacco Control gave national health ministries political cover and legal tools they had previously lacked. None of these were sufficient on their own. It was the combination that worked, albeit slowly. The same limit appears in antitrust. The 1911 breakup of Standard Oil is cited as the definitive remedy, but several successor companies immediately reconsolidated, and John D. Rockefeller’s personal fortune increased after the breakup as the stock prices of the subsidiaries rose (Stoller 2019). The remedy addressed the legal structure of the monopoly without altering the underlying concentration of power.
Some market structures build harm in by design. The tontine from the markets chapter—a pooled investment governments banned for rewarding the last survivor for the others’ deaths— reappears in the platform race to be the last surviving competitor.
Capture is the recurring enemy, and it has an international cousin. When Australia required plain packaging for cigarettes, Philip Morris restructured its holdings through a Hong Kong subsidiary to sue under an investor-state dispute settlement clause— a move so transparently opportunistic that even the arbitrators were not impressed. Regulatory capture also has an extreme form. In South Korea, chaebol executives were convicted and then pardoned as too important to the economy to jail. “Too big to jail” is not a technology-industry invention.
Capture also has a technical form. In the savings and loan crisis of the 1980s, control fraud—executives using their control of a company to route contracts to related parties and manipulate reported earnings— was made possible by deregulation that removed oversight and by accounting standards that gave executives wide latitude (Black 2005). The auditors who certified the books were paid by the companies they audited, which gave them a powerful reason not to find problems. The same structure produced Wirecard decades later.
The enforcement machinery can also be theater. The EU’s record fine against Google of €4.34 billion for Android antitrust violations in 2018 amounted to roughly two weeks of Google’s annual profit at the time. Google appealed, had the fine reduced slightly, and continued the practices it had been fined for. A fine that is smaller than the profit from the conduct is not a deterrent; it is a licensing fee.

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.7 Moral Panics and Wrong Diagnoses
A moral panic is a disproportionate, often exaggerated public alarm that can coexist with a real harm— and often targets the wrong harm while leaving the real one unaddressed. The lineage runs through dime novels in the 1880s, Fredric Wertham’s Seduction of the Innocent against comics in the 1950s (Wertham 1954), rock music, and Dungeons and Dragons, before arriving at violent video games in the 1990s. Wertham’s testimony brought comic books before a Senate subcommittee in 1954 and led directly to the Comics Code Authority, a self-regulatory body that banned dark content so comprehensively that it effectively gutted the medium for a generation. Video games arrived in force in 1993, when a Senate subcommittee held hearings focused on two games: Mortal Kombat, which allowed players to rip an opponent’s spine out as a finishing move, and Night Trap, which featured vampires draining blood from actresses. The hearings generated excellent television and led directly to the creation of the Entertainment Software Rating Board, the voluntary age-based rating system still in use today.
The video-game panic is the clearest modern example. Dave Grossman offered a more careful version of the alarm. His claim rested on military training research: fewer than a quarter of soldiers in World War II actually fired their weapons in combat, so the Army redesigned its training using operant conditioning with human-silhouette targets to raise that rate in Korea and Vietnam. Violent video games applied the same conditioning to children without consent or any ethical framework. Unlike the public panic, his argument was internally coherent. Unfortunately, the scientific literature did not validate it.
After Columbine, legislators went after games, but the scientific literature never supported the hypothesis: laboratory measures of aggression bear little relationship to real-world violence, and large longitudinal studies consistently find no meaningful effect (Ferguson 2015). The simplest check is cross-national: Japan and South Korea are among the highest per-capita consumers of video games in the world and have dramatically lower rates of violent crime than the United States. Gun availability, inequality, and the history of racially organized violence explain American violence far better than games do, but they are much harder to face.
In 2011 the Supreme Court settled the legal question, if not the empirical one. California had enacted a law restricting the sale of violent video games to minors. The Court struck it down in Brown v. Entertainment Merchants Association, applying the same First Amendment analysis it would apply to books or films. The majority noted that the research California presented did not establish a causal link between violent games and harm to minors, and that the burden of proof for restricting expression falls on those who seek restriction.
By then the panic was already fading, displaced by fresh anxieties about social media and smartphones. What had not faded were the harms the panic had never addressed. While legislators debated spine-ripping finishing moves, the real harm went largely unregulated: loot boxes, randomized rewards purchased with real money, marketed to children, and now recognized as gambling by several European regulators.

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.8 The Bridge
Social-media and AI harms are pollution-model harms. The trap is to respond with moral-panic framing—“ban the kids’ phones”— instead of diagnosing the actual harm: attention extraction, addictive design, discrimination, and surveillance. Regulating well means diagnosing the real harm rather than the one that generates the best testimony, using the pollution and product-safety models where they fit, and defending the regulator from capture. The European Union’s Digital Markets Act, which forces designated gatekeepers to allow interoperability and forbids self-preferencing, and India’s Unified Payments Interface, which built public payment rails before any private platform could achieve lock-in, are two early examples of regulation aimed at the actual source of the harm. Regulation has also moved faster than the industry claims is possible. The EU AI Act requires transparency for high-risk systems, mandates human oversight for consequential automated decisions, and bans specific applications outright. Before the GDPR took effect in 2018, industry associations described it as unworkable and predicted that it would destroy European tech competitiveness. By 2024 it had generated approximately $4 billion in fines and had changed how companies worldwide handle personal data, including companies with no European operations that simply chose to comply rather than maintain two systems. The argument that AI regulation will destroy innovation has been made about every major technology regulation in living memory, and has been wrong every time. The question is not whether the harms can be named; it is whether the people who benefit from them can be made to pay.






NoteTakeaway



Harm is not a fact that precedes regulation; it is a claim made by the powerful, the panicked, and the organized. Regulating well means diagnosing the actual harm rather than the one that generates the best testimony, using the pollution and product-safety models where they fit, and defending the regulator from capture.

title: 7  Regulation
text:
7.9 Exercises

Rank the harms, then the laws.

Consider the list “alcohol, cannabis, heroin, gambling, social media, AI-generated misinformation”. Rank the items by measured harm, then by how the law actually treats them. Discuss the gaps and what explains them.

Two models of harm.

Pick a harm (e.g., a bridge collapse, leaded gasoline, a data breach, or teen anxiety from Instagram). Classify it as rare-dramatic-attributable or diffuse-cumulative, and say which regulatory instrument each model naturally suggests. Which model were you trained to think in?

Moral panic vs. real harm.

Choose a concern (violent video games, kids and phones, “AI will end humanity”). List the features that make it look like a moral panic and the features that make it an evidence-backed harm. What is the actual harm the panic may be distracting from?

Precautionary vs. wait-and-see.

Replay the thalidomide decision: you are the regulator with evidence that is suggestive but not conclusive. Do you approve or wait? What does your answer imply for “move fast and break things” and for releasing open-weight AI models?

Redesign the law.

Pick a harm currently regulated on a moral or panic basis rather than an evidence basis (e.g., cannabis, a social-media feature). Propose a regulation that tracks the actual harm, and name the political obstacles to passing it.

Beat the playbook.

You are the regulator and the industry is running the five-step uncertainty playbook. For each step, name one counter-move (independent funding, burden-of-proof rules, naming the front groups, deadlines).

Settlement or solution.

Study the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement. Why did a $206 billion settlement fail to end the tobacco problem? What would a solution have required, and why was a settlement the outcome the parties preferred?

title: 8  Change
text:
8.1 How Change Happens
Name one thing that is better now than it was fifty years ago. Now ask who made it better, and how. Gay marriage is legal in more places than it was, the ozone hole is closing, cars have seatbelts, and far fewer people die in factory fires than did in 1911. None of these things happened by themselves, and none of them happened because the people with power were persuaded. They happened because organized groups applied sustained pressure over time, and they rarely happen any other way.
The historical record is consistent across very different contexts. Change happens when three things come together: organization, opportunity, and framing. The civil rights movement, environmental regulation, seat belts, tobacco control, marriage equality, and worker safety all followed this pattern— slow, non-linear, and won by pressure rather than persuasion alone. The popular story that Rosa Parks was a spontaneous individual is factually wrong: she was an NAACP officer chosen as a plaintiff deliberately, and the bus boycott that followed was coordinated by hundreds of people whose names are not remembered (the conclusion opens with the fuller story) (Beckerman 2022).
John Kingdon gave the pattern a precise description (Kingdon 1995). Change becomes possible when three streams align: a problem defined as a crisis, a politics stream with a constituency and a mood, and a policy stream containing a ready-made solution. The window opens rarely and closes quickly, so the people who want change must have built the solution before the problem becomes undeniable.
Three mechanisms illustrate how this works in practice. ACT UP, founded in 1987, used direct action to accelerate drug approval, targeting the FDA and pharmaceutical companies until they changed their timelines— a demonstration that the process of regulation itself can be shifted by organized pressure. The abolitionist movement distributed slave narratives such as Olaudah Equiano’s 1789 narrative and Frederick Douglass’s 1845 memoir, making suffering imaginable to readers who had never seen it, and ran the 1790s sugar boycott as the first mass consumer boycott in British history (Hochschild 2006). And Kerala, in southern India, won land reform in 1969 not through occupation but through election, breaking the veto of the landlord class and unlocking decades of gains in literacy and life expectancy (Drèze and Sen 2013).
There is also a quieter side to the record. Erica Chenoweth found that campaigns engaging the active participation of roughly 3.5 percent of a population have repeatedly been enough to force change (Chenoweth and Stephan 2011). In a city of half a million people, that is seventeen thousand people doing something instead of just complaining. And the capacity for that something is real. After the 1917 Halifax explosion and Hurricane Katrina, ordinary people organized mutual aid with remarkable speed and generosity, even as authorities and media reported violence that later investigation showed never happened (Solnit 2009; Quarantelli 1998). The capacity is there; the question is whether it is organized.

title: 8  Change
text:
8.2 Worker Power
Worker power is the clearest example of gains that were won, not conceded. The Combination Acts criminalized unions in Britain; the Tolpuddle Martyrs were transported to Australia for forming one; the 1926 General Strike was defeated; and Thatcher spent a decade breaking what remained. The eight-hour day did not arrive because employers became convinced workers deserved it; it arrived after the First World War, when the fear of revolution made the cost of continued resistance higher than the cost of concession. The Melbourne stonemasons won the first eight-hour day in 1856 not through moral persuasion but by applying collective leverage at a moment of their opponents’ weakness.
The demand was older than the Melbourne victory. Robert Owen had called for “eight hours labour, eight hours recreation, eight hours rest” in 1817, but Owen could not make it happen through goodwill and argument. It took workers who understood that argument only mattered when backed by the capacity to impose costs. In May 1886, a general strike for the eight-hour day shut down factories across the United States. On May 4, a bomb exploded in Haymarket Square during a protest in Chicago, killing both police officers and civilians. The bomb-thrower was never identified, but eight anarchists were tried anyway, and four were hanged. The Haymarket affair became a rallying point for the international labor movement; May Day was adopted as a workers’ holiday across most of the world, with the notable exception of the United States and Canada, which moved their Labor Day to September specifically to avoid the association. In 1889, the newly formed Second International declared May 1 an international day of solidarity for the eight-hour day. But spreading a demand and achieving it are different things. In most countries, forty years passed between the first serious campaigns and its legal establishment. What closed the gap was not sympathy but the end of the First World War, a political crisis severe enough that governments feared revolution. France legislated the eight-hour day in April 1919. Britain passed the Hours of Work Convention that same year. The first convention adopted by the International Labour Organization in 1919 was an eight-hour day and forty-eight hour week for industrial workers. Then and now, labor gains were not won because employers became convinced that workers deserved better. They were won because the cost of continued resistance exceeded the cost of concession.
The same lesson runs through the Triangle Shirtwaist fire. On March 25, 1911, a fire broke out on the eighth floor of a building in Greenwich Village. The managers had locked the stairwell doors to prevent unauthorized breaks and theft. 146 workers died, most of them young immigrant women, many Jewish and Italian. Some jumped from the windows. The owners were acquitted of manslaughter and collected the insurance. The conditions were standard practice: locked exits, no sprinklers, overcrowding, abusive supervisors. What was not standard was the combination of a catastrophic death toll and the organizational capacity that existed to exploit the political opening. The Women’s Trade Union League, the International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union, and the socialist press had spent years building that capacity. Within days, Rose Schneiderman gave a speech that reframed the debate: this was not a tragedy but a crime, and the perpetrators were not the invisible people who set fires but the visible people who locked the doors and blocked regulation. The result was a legislative investigation that produced fifty-six pieces of legislation over three years, covering fire safety, working hours, factory inspection, and child labor. The fire itself did not produce the laws; it was the fire plus organized political capacity.
The institutions that made these gains stick were deliberately built. German codetermination puts workers on corporate supervisory boards, half of them in large firms. Australia’s Harvester judgment of 1907 established a “basic wage” through a system of arbitration rather than bargaining alone. And COSATU, the South African trade-union federation, was a decisive force in ending apartheid. Australia’s Conciliation and Arbitration Act of 1904 built a labor system unlike either the British or German models. A federal industrial court, not collective bargaining, set wages and conditions through legally binding awards that applied across whole industries. The 1907 Harvester judgment established the “basic wage” as the minimum needed to support a family in frugal comfort. Union membership was high because belonging to a union was a condition of accessing the award system, not because workers had achieved industrial leverage through organizing. New Zealand took a similar path: compulsory arbitration from 1894, the eight-hour day for most workers in 1891, and old-age pensions by 1898, thirty-seven years before the United States got Social Security. These systems were dismantled during the 1990s under market liberalization, replaced by enterprise bargaining that produced wider variation in wages and conditions.
Employers have also learned how to prevent organizing. High individual compensation is the most direct approach: workers paid well relative to their labor-market alternatives have less to gain from collective bargaining. Union avoidance is a formal management discipline with a consulting industry behind it: labor relations firms advise employers on how to structure workplaces and compensation to prevent the conditions under which organizing becomes attractive. The legal boundary between employee and contractor is another tool: reclassifying workers as independent contractors removes them from the framework that protects organizing activity. The pattern persists today. When the Rana Plaza factory collapse killed 1,134 garment workers in 2013, it produced the Bangladesh Accord, a real gain, then weakened, then re-won— two steps forward, one step back.

title: 8  Change
text:
8.3 The Technologist’s Role
Technologists hold unusual cards. Their skills are scarce, they have access to systems that others cannot see, and they carry inside knowledge of how the machinery actually works. They also face real constraints: contracts, career risk, and the ideology of neutrality that says an engineer’s job is to build, not to choose. Erin Cech calls the ideology the passion principle: “do what you love” is converted into a reason to accept extraction, and its Japanese endpoint is karoshi, death from overwork (Cech 2021). The passion principle falls hardest on workers from less privileged backgrounds, who have the most to lose from accepting its terms. Workers from more privileged backgrounds can absorb the costs of passion-coded careers: family wealth provides a cushion, networks provide alternative paths, and prior social capital makes it easier to exit without losing everything. For workers without those resources, the passion principle extracts years of discounted labor before returning them to the general labor market with depleted savings and credentials that do not transfer. Precarious workers like gig workers and seasonal workers are hit hardest. Organizing takes time they may not have, and requires a willingness to accept the risk of termination that workers without income security cannot absorb. Many are formally classified as independent contractors, which in most jurisdictions removes them from the legal framework that protects organizing. The legal boundary between employee and contractor has been contested in dozens of jurisdictions, with outcomes that vary and have been inconsistent even within jurisdictions. Over and over, rules are rewritten to ensure that the workers most exposed to poor conditions are least able to fight back (Jaffe 2021; Kelly 2022). The software-engineering literature is a symptom of the same blind spot: it covers architecture and management extensively but has almost nothing to say about workers’ rights or cooperatives, the way medicine once hid its own error rate. Medicine’s encounter with its own error rate is a case study in professional taboo. For most of the twentieth century, the dominant framework for medical error was individual blame: a bad outcome was the fault of a bad physician, and the appropriate response was to identify and punish the individual. This framework served the profession’s interest in self-regulation and resisted external oversight. The finding that between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans died annually from preventable medical errors was not new to researchers, but it was taboo because it endangered the profession as a whole. Aviation-style checklists, which treat error as a predictable product of complex systems, were resisted for decades by physicians who experienced them as an affront to professional judgment. The evidence that checklists reduced deaths was not in dispute. The resistance was to the implication that standardized protocols should constrain clinical practice. Software engineering has its equivalent silences. The books cover project management, architecture, team dynamics, and career development. They do not cover workers’ rights, noncompete agreements, ownership of employee inventions, alternative ownership structures, or the systematic harassment and exclusion of women. The topics placed out of bounds are those that, if examined, would reveal tensions in the profession’s self-understanding or power structure. The placement of a boundary is a form of power.
The leverage is not theoretical. In 2023, the Writers Guild of America struck for five months and won explicit contract language that AI cannot write or rewrite scripts, and that scripts cannot be used to train AI systems (Kelly 2022). No individual writer could have secured that alone. The Screen Actors Guild reached a parallel agreement that included restrictions on the digital replication of performers’ likenesses without ongoing consent. These victories established enforceable contractual limits on what employers could do with AI— limits that individual workers negotiating alone could never have secured. Regulation has also moved faster than the industry claims is possible. The EU AI Act requires transparency for high-risk systems, mandates human oversight for consequential automated decisions, and bans specific applications outright. The GDPR, dismissed as unworkable before 2018, had by 2024 changed how companies worldwide handle personal data—the regulation chapter gives the numbers. Technologists can refuse, whistleblow, organize, build alternatives, or work on policy, and each of those is a form of pressure.

title: 8  Change
text:
8.4 The Reform Menu
The menu of possible responses is not mysterious. Transparency and audits make harms visible; liability makes them costly; structural remedies such as interoperability and breakups attack the concentration itself; worker power changes who has a seat at the table; public alternatives remove the need to beg; and global coordination handles harms that cross borders.
Each has a capture risk, and each has an existence proof. Japan’s postwar land reform seized agricultural land from landlords and sold it to the tenant farmers who worked it, an expropriation that broke the landlord class and set the stage for industrialization (Studwell 2013). South Korea and Taiwan followed the same template at almost exactly the same time, for the same Cold War reasons. In South Korea, the Land Reform Act of 1950 capped landholdings and required excess land to be sold to the state for redistribution to tenant farmers. In Taiwan, the program between 1949 and 1953 transferred land from Taiwanese landlords to the tenant farmers who cultivated it. The compensation paid to landlords was structured in ways that made delay expensive: bonds whose value eroded, or equity in state enterprises whose worth depended on policies the landlords no longer controlled. The design was intentional: reform administrators understood that the landlord class would use any instrument available to reverse the transfer. The reforms created the conditions for subsequent industrial policies to succeed, because the rural population had both the stability and the incentive to participate in markets rather than spending their energy surviving extraction.
The words “land reform” have also been used to describe something very different. Stalin’s forced collectivization of Soviet agriculture between 1929 and 1933 drove peasants into collective farms at gunpoint, killed or deported millions labeled “kulaks” for owning a cow or two, and caused a famine that killed somewhere between five and eight million people in Ukraine alone. Mao’s collectivization in China followed the same blueprint with worse results. The Great Leap Forward forced peasants into communes, requisitioned grain even as harvests failed, and caused a famine that killed an estimated thirty to forty-five million people. These programs had nothing in common with the reforms described above. Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and Kerala gave farmers ownership of the land they worked. Stalin and Mao abolished private ownership entirely and replaced it with state control enforced by violence, combined with the systematic destruction of any incentive to grow food. Critics who invoke collectivization to argue against democratic land reform are comparing policies that created owner-farmers with policies that destroyed them. The Montreal Protocol worked where other environmental agreements failed because it combined a binding agreement, differentiated obligations, a technology-transfer fund, and trade sanctions against non-participants (Parson 2003). The European Union’s Digital Markets Act of 2024 forces designated gatekeepers to allow interoperability and forbids self-preferencing, with fines of up to 20 percent of global revenue. India’s UPI and Brazil’s Pix built public payment rails before any private platform could achieve lock-in. And the yakuza, Japan’s organized crime syndicates, shrank from roughly 180,000 members in the 1960s to under 20,000 by the 2020s not because they became less useful, but because a sustained political decision made the cost of associating with them prohibitive. A structurally powerful industry can be made a source of vulnerability.
Concrete democratic reforms have also worked. Ranked-choice voting in Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, and more than a dozen US cities has produced legislatures that more closely reflect what voters actually want. Independent redistricting commissions have measurably reduced partisan gerrymandering in Arizona, California, and Michigan. New York City’s public matching funds for small donations have shifted the incentive structure for candidates, making it possible to run a competitive campaign on small contributions rather than depending on a handful of major donors. Broad constitutional reform through sustained public participation succeeded in Iceland following the 2008 financial crisis. Campaigns that engaged roughly 3.5 percent of a population have been sufficient to force change in case after case.

title: 8  Change
text:
8.5 Alternatives That Scaled
The claim that alternatives cannot work at scale is false, and the counterexamples are large enough to have annual reports. In 1956, a Catholic priest named José María Arizmendiarrieta gathered five workers in a converted school in Mondragón, in the Basque region of Spain, and started making paraffin heaters. By 2024, the Mondragón Corporation employed roughly 80,000 people across manufacturing, retail, financial services, and education. Its workers own the enterprise. They elect the management, negotiate pay scales internally, and when Spain’s economy collapsed after 2008, Mondragón moved workers between cooperatives rather than letting them go (Morrison 1991).
In the 1860s, Friedrich Raiffeisen was running a rural municipality in what is now Germany and watching small farmers get crushed by moneylenders. He organized the farmers to lend to each other. Members pooled deposits, the cooperative extended credit at rates commercial lenders could not match, and the surplus stayed within the cooperative. Today the Raiffeisen network is one of Europe’s largest banking groups, and the World Council of Credit Unions estimates that roughly a billion people worldwide are members of credit cooperatives of one kind or another (Whyte and Whyte 1991).
Vienna in the 1920s faced a housing crisis that would look familiar to anyone paying rent in a large city today. The Social Democratic city government decided to treat housing as a public utility rather than a market good. Between 1923 and 1934, the city built roughly 60,000 apartments in large municipal complexes called the Gemeindebau. They were substantial brick buildings with courtyards, laundries, libraries, kindergartens, and clinics. The Karl-Marx-Hof, completed in 1930, is over a kilometer long. The program was funded by a progressive tax on luxury goods: people buying fur coats and racehorses paid for workers to have decent apartments. The city still owns about 220,000 apartments directly and subsidizes roughly another 200,000 through a nonprofit cooperative sector. About 60 percent of Vienna’s residents live in subsidized housing of one kind or another, and rents are set by law rather than by the market.
Amul is an Indian dairy cooperative founded in 1946 in Gujarat after farmers organized to break the monopoly of a single private contractor who controlled their access to the Bombay milk market. Today Amul is the world’s largest dairy cooperative by volume, collecting milk from roughly 3.6 million farmer-members. Canada’s Desjardins, founded in 1900 by a journalist named Alphonse Desjardins, is now one of the largest financial institutions in Canada, with roughly eight million members and assets over 400 billion Canadian dollars. Members own it, members elect the board, and surplus is returned to members. It survived the 2008 financial crisis in considerably better shape than many of the shareholder-owned banks.

title: 8  Change
text:
8.6 Five Tools
The finale of this workshop offers an alternative taxonomy of the reform menu: five tools that have historically done the work. Collective organizing means building institutions that can act in coordination. Regulatory pressure means participating in the slow work of making rules. Alternative structures means building existence proofs that the current arrangement is not the only one: Mondragón has run as a worker cooperative for nearly seventy years, Vienna’s Gemeindebau still houses working-class families a century on, Amul coordinates 3.6 million farmer-members, and Desjardins serves roughly eight million members and survived 2008 in considerably better shape than the big banks. Strategic communication means engaging with the psychology of belief change, because facts do not change contested minds—stories told by trusted messengers do. And sustained participation means showing up for decades: the Federalist Society built its judicial pipeline over forty years, and the labor movement built the eight-hour day over the same span.
This is the hardest part of the message for people accustomed to fast feedback loops. No single action produces structural change; what produces it is organizational capacity built before the political opening arrives, and the willingness to use that capacity when the opening comes. Refusing to vote or join a union is a political act, and refusing to engage simply delegates the decision to whoever will. How society works is knowable, and knowing it is the prerequisite for changing it.






NoteTakeaway



The harms are not mysterious and the responses are not untried. Every tool discussed in the workshop is available to people who organize. Technologists hold real cards; the question is whether they play them.

title: 8  Change
text:
8.7 Exercises

Policy-window map.

Pick one concrete harm. For Kingdon’s three streams: assess whether a window is open and what would open it.

Coalition design.

Choose a reform (e.g., mandatory algorithmic audits). List likely supporters, likely opponents, and the unexpected allies (parents, small business, civil-liberty groups, religious communities) that could make it a winning coalition.

Leverage inventory.

As a technologist, list your specific sources of leverage (skills, access, capital, community) and one concrete action you could take in each of the next 1, 6, and 12 months.

Harm-to-lesson mapping.

Take one harm (e.g., AI-driven hiring discrimination) and write one sentence connecting it to each lesson. The point is to demonstrate that every real harm has structural, economic, psychological, stratificational, regulatory, and ideological dimensions.

Reform-menu debate.

Assign groups different positions (e.g., audits only, liability, breakups, public options, worker power, “it cannot be fixed”). Each group argues its case; then the room discusses which combination is realistic and coherent.

Backward plan.

Pick a target outcome five years out (e.g., “audits of high-impact models are mandatory and meaningful”). Work backward to name the milestones, coalitions, and political conditions required at each stage.

Worker-power audit.

Choose one workplace harm (surveillance, deskilling, on-call exhaustion, pay opacity). Which of the worker-power institutions (codetermination, sectoral bargaining, arbitration, a union) would address it, and who would have to move first?

Five tools.

Take a single reform (e.g., algorithmic audits) and map it onto the five tools—collective organizing, regulatory pressure, alternative structures, strategic communication, sustained participation. Which tool is missing from most tech-industry versions of this plan?

title: 9  Conclusion
text:
9.1 Moral Reframing in Practice
The dominant popular narrative about social change centers on individuals: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat and the Civil Rights Movement was born. This narrative is factually wrong and strategically disabling. Rosa Parks was the secretary of the Montgomery chapter of the NAACP and had recently attended the Highlander Folk School, a training center for labor and civil rights organizers. The Montgomery Bus Boycott that followed her arrest was organized by the Montgomery Improvement Association, coordinated carpools across a city for over a year, and was sustained by the labor of hundreds of people whose names are not remembered. The choice of Parks as the plaintiff in the subsequent legal case was deliberate: other potential plaintiffs had been rejected as less strategically suitable. This is what organized political campaigns look like. The reduction of that campaign to one person’s spontaneous act of courage makes it both more inspiring and less useful as a model.
The most rigorous quantitative analysis of social change I know of is Erica Chenoweth and Maria Stephan’s study of 323 resistance campaigns between 1900 and 2006 (Chenoweth and Stephan 2011). They found that nonviolent campaigns succeeded roughly twice as often as violent ones, and that the threshold for success was consistent: campaigns that engaged the active participation of roughly 3.5% of the population did not fail. The mechanism is not mysterious. Nonviolent campaigns can recruit from a broader population, including people who will not take up arms but will march, boycott, strike, or withdraw labor. Broader participation creates broader legitimacy and makes it harder for the state to frame repression as protecting order rather than suppressing dissent. The 3.5% figure is not a guarantee; it describes a historical pattern. But it is a more useful starting point than the assumption that popular majorities produce change automatically.
Economic disruption is the mechanism that connects organized pressure to actual policy change. The Montgomery Bus Boycott worked because it destroyed the bus company’s revenue from its Black ridership. The South African divestment campaign worked because it raised the cost of the apartheid state’s international borrowing. In each case the mechanism was economic: the people in power faced a cost-benefit calculation that changed. Moral suasion may have affected some individuals. It did not change the structural calculation that drove policy.
Moral arguments have a poor track record as the primary lever of social change. They aren’t irrelevant: they build coalitions, provide the framework that justifies what a movement is asking for, and affect potential participants’ willingness to accept personal costs. But moral arguments addressed to those in power, without the economic or political pressure that makes their rejection costly, consistently fail. The tobacco industry did not voluntarily stop marketing cigarettes to children because public health advocates published articles about harm. Corporate privacy practices do not change because researchers demonstrate the extent of surveillance. What changes the behavior of those who benefit from a harmful arrangement is when not changing becomes more costly than changing.
The criminalization of homosexuality through sodomy laws is often treated as an ancient prejudice that modernity finally overcame, but its legal form is specific and recent. The British Offences Against the Person Act of 1861 and the Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1885 (under which Oscar Wilde was prosecuted) established the statutory framework that then spread through British colonial law to India, Kenya, Singapore, and dozens of other territories. This was a Victorian legal export, not a timeless human universal.
The Stonewall uprising in June 1969 catalyzed what followed, but that “what” was organized political work: building community institutions, litigating against discriminatory laws, lobbying legislatures, training activists, and making the case for rights in terms that demanded equal treatment rather than tolerance (Hirshman 2012). The AIDS crisis beginning in the early 1980s devastated these communities. ACT UP, founded in 1987, developed direct action tactics that accelerated drug approval timelines, targeting the FDA, pharmaceutical companies, and media coverage. In doing so, they changed what was considered acceptable activist pressure on public health institutions. The movement that emerged from the AIDS years was more sophisticated, better organized, and more willing to engage in explicit political conflict than it had been (Faderman 2015).
Legal change did not arrive at once. Each step was criticized as premature by conservatives and inadequate by the communities affected, but each made the next one thinkable. Marriage equality, which seemed to most observers politically unreachable in 2000, was recognized by the US Supreme Court in 2015. The speed of that final sequence reflects both the sustained organizing of prior decades and specific features of the American constitutional system that allowed judicial strategy to outpace legislative consensus.
What these changes reveal about how moral consensus shifts is that the process has identifiable components. Changed facts matter: the AIDS epidemic made invisible communities visible in ways that shifted public sympathy and political calculation. Changed visibility matters: LGBTQ+ people in prominent public roles before and after coming out reduced the distance between the abstract policy debate and human recognition. Organized political pressure matters: neither marriage equality nor any other major rights advance arrived without sustained campaigns that built coalitions, litigated strategically, and maintained pressure across decades of partial progress and setback. Finally, legal strategy matters: advocates have to choose which cases to bring, in which courts, at which moment (Hannig 2023).

title: 9  Conclusion
text:
9.2 The Expanding Circle
The circle of people we recognize as fully human has expanded over the last two and a half centuries. It has happened slowly, and with catastrophic reversals, but through mechanisms that are identifiable and replicable.
The historian Lynn Hunt points to something unexpected: novels (Hunt 2007). The eighteenth century saw an explosion of epistolary fiction (i.e., novels written as letters) that asked readers to inhabit the inner life of someone unlike themselves, to feel the world from inside another person’s consciousness. Hunt argues that this trained readers to recognize the humanity of strangers and understand that other people’s interior lives were as real as their own. Whether novels were a cause or a symptom of changing attitudes is debatable, but slave narratives in the nineteenth century worked on the same principle. The Interesting Narrative of Olaudah Equiano (1789) and Frederick Douglass’s Narrative (1845) put readers inside an enslaved person’s experience in a way that statistics never could. The abolitionist movement distributed these books deliberately and widely. Making suffering something a reader from a comfortable life could imaginatively enter was a political strategy (Hochschild 2006).
A second mechanism is organized political pressure. The Somerset case in Britain in 1772 illustrates how this works. James Somerset was an enslaved man brought to England who escaped and was recaptured by his enslaver. His case was taken up by abolitionists, who argued that English common law did not support slavery. Lord Mansfield’s ruling said only that Somerset could not be forcibly transported out of England, but abolitionists used it as a wedge. They had already built a network of committees, pamphlets, and petitions. The boycott of West Indian sugar in the 1790s was the first mass consumer boycott in British history. These campaigns eventually produced the Slave Trade Act of 1807 and the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833. The expansion of the moral circle, here, was not a spontaneous change of heart by elites. It was the result of sustained, organized work by people who built coalitions, applied pressure across decades, and framed their arguments in terms their opponents could not easily dismiss.
The expansion of the moral circle has never been linear. Reconstruction in the United States after the Civil War extended legal rights to formerly enslaved people, but was then systematically dismantled through paramilitary violence, electoral manipulation, and judicial capitulation. Most of the gains of the 1860s and 1870s were reversed by 1900. It took another sixty years, and another sustained organizing campaign, to recover them in formal law. The current rollback of rights for trans people in several countries is not an anomaly. Every extension of the moral circle has produced a counter-movement arguing that the extension is too far, too fast, or aimed at the wrong people. Sometimes those counter-movements win, at least for a while.
The relevance to technology is direct, even if the industry has largely avoided the conversation. Every system that makes decisions about people embeds assumptions about whose interests count and whose harm is legible. Facial recognition systems that perform poorly on darker skin tones are not neutral tools that happen to malfunction for some users. They encode a prior judgment about whose face needs to be recognized accurately. Content moderation systems that work better in English than in Amharic or Tagalog reflect a prior judgment about whose speech deserves moderation resources. Peter Singer argued that reason itself pushes in this direction: once you accept that suffering matters, it becomes harder to explain why only the suffering of people like you matters. That logical pressure is real, but it does not do this work on its own. Someone has to organize the campaign, draft the legislation, build the coalition, and be prepared to keep going when the counter-movement wins the next election (Singer 1981).

title: 9  Conclusion
text:
9.3 Five Tools
The preceding chapters have argued that large-scale harm is produced by systems with structural incentives to produce it, and those systems change when organized groups impose sustained economic or political costs on them. That argument implies that individual ethical consumption, career choices, and personal commitments matter to the people who make them, but are not the mechanism by which industries get regulated or power gets redistributed. Five tools have historically accomplished that; the previous chapter gives the full case for each.
Collective organizing means building institutions with the capacity to act in coordination. The 2023 Writers Guild of America strike demonstrated that workers can negotiate explicit contractual limits on how AI is used against them that no individual writer could have secured alone.
Regulatory pressure means participating in the political processes through which rules get made: litigation, lobbying, public comment, and electoral organizing. None of these are glamorous, and most of them are slow. The tobacco case took forty years from the first clear science to a partial legal settlement.
Alternative structures means building institutions that demonstrate other models are possible. Mondragón has been running for nearly seventy years. The Viennese Gemeindebau has housed working-class families for a century. Credit unions serve roughly a billion people worldwide. The claim that shareholder capitalism is the only workable model for large-scale enterprise is empirically false.
Strategic communication means engaging seriously with the psychology of belief change. Facts do not change minds in contested domains; stories told by trusted messengers do. This is not a counsel of manipulation. It is a recognition that if you want to change what people believe about AI regulation, platform power, or labor rights, you need to find people whose social worlds already include such conversations, meet them where they are, and make updating their beliefs consistent with rather than threatening to their identities.
Sustained participation means showing up repeatedly over years. The Federalist Society built its judicial pipeline over forty years. The labor movement built the eight-hour day over forty years. The LGBTQ+ rights movement built toward marriage equality over forty years. This is the part of the agenda that is most difficult to communicate to people who are accustomed to fast feedback loops. No single action produces structural change. What produces structural change is organizational capacity built before a political opening arrives, and the willingness to use that capacity when the opening comes.

title: 9  Conclusion
text:
9.4 What We Can Defend
Years ago, while hiking in the woods, I spotted a set of bamboo windchimes hanging from a tree. There were five weather-stained rods carved to different lengths, each of which had initials carved on it and a pair of dates. I can’t remember the years exactly—this was back in the days of chemical cameras, so if I still have the photo I took it’s in a box in my basement—but I remember they ran from the 1930s and 1940s to the 1980s.
The bar the chimes hung from had a hole carved in it for a sixth. I still sometimes wonder why it was missing. Had a squirrel chewed through the twine used to tie it on, so that it fell into the undergrowth and was lost? Had someone’s time not come yet? Or had there been no one left who knew or cared to add it?
After all I’ve read, I believe that caring about the future is a personal choice, and that the most defensible version of our obligation to it is simple: don’t foreclose options. I think we should strive to give our grandchildren, and their grandchildren, as many choices as we had. They should be able to enjoy the things that we can enjoy, like safe drinking water, healthy coral reefs, and free elections. I believe that we don’t own those things. We are just their trustees, and like all trustees, we are accountable for what we hand on, even if the beneficiaries aren’t in the room.

title: 9  Conclusion
text:
9.5 Where Do We Start?
At work, the most immediate choices are about what to build and who to build it for. These chapters have described how products encode assumptions about whose harm is legible and whose is not, and about whose data is worth protecting and whose can be extracted, packaged, and sold. Asking those questions explicitly in design reviews and sprint retrospectives and architecture discussions is a step toward change. It is not sufficient on its own, but it is not nothing. After all, every major organizational harm documented in these chapters was produced by organizations full of people who did not ask these questions.
If your company has a union or a worker advocacy group, joining it is the highest-leverage individual action available. If it does not, it’s worth remembering that the tech workers who have organized in recent years did so the same way everyone else has: by finding other people who shared their concerns and committing to sustained collective action. (It’s also worth remembering that Google’s cafeteria workers organized while the engineers were still debating whether it was “appropriate”.)
In community, you may already be doing something valuable, like showing up at a literacy program or helping at a food bank. Libraries, community environmental groups, and other civic organizations are where the capacity for political action gets built. The Montgomery Bus Boycott was organized by people who knew each other from church, and the abolitionist movement in Britain by people who knew each other from Quaker meetings. The specific institution matters less than the sustained, repeated contact that allows people to build trust and coordinate action (Beckerman 2022).
Politically, the most useful question is not “which party should I vote for?” but “where can I apply organized pressure most effectively?” Electoral organizing matters, but so does showing up to public comment periods, participating in professional associations that engage with regulation, and joining organizations that are doing the sustained work of advocacy on issues that are more specific than a party platform. The 3.5% threshold cited earlier is not an abstraction: in a city of half a million people, it is seventeen thousand people doing something instead of just complaining.

title: 9  Conclusion
text:
9.6 A Closing Note
The tech industry isn’t as new or as revolutionary as it pretends to be. It is an industry with the same structural pressures, the same political dynamics, and the same aversion to regulation as every industry before it. Decisions with consequences for billions of people are being made by a small number of unaccountable billionaires.
But I am not finished being hopeful. Change is hard, but not impossible. Gay marriage is legal. The ozone hole is closing, and the world is building solar power faster than anyone imagined was possible.
We are not going to solve big problems alone. We are going to have to work with people we disagree with, accept partial victories, and keep going after setbacks. We are going to have to be patient and organized and strategic, which feels much less satisfying than righteous anger.
But we already know how to build things. We know how to think about systems and debug complex interactions. The political and social systems these chapters have described are not more complex than the technical systems we work with. They are just harder to test.
So: start where you are, use what you have, help who you can.
